qs.q: A 52-year-old woman with early menopause and troublesome menopausal symptoms is considered for hormone replacement therapy (HRT). What is the primary indication for HRT in this patient?
o: Prevention of metastatic bone disease progression in postmenopausal women
Prevention of osteoporosis and treatment of menopausal symptoms in early menopause
First-line long-term maintenance in older women with established osteoporosis
Permanent suppression of osteoblastic activity in patients with bone loss
qs.e: HRT is primarily indicated for the prevention of osteoporosis in women with an early menopause and for treatment of women with osteoporosis in their early fifties who have troublesome menopausal symptoms. It should be avoided in older women with established osteoporosis due to risks of breast cancer and cardiovascular disease.

qs.q: A 55-year-old postmenopausal woman discusses long-term options for fracture prevention. Why is hormone replacement therapy no longer recommended as a first-line approach for treating osteoporosis?
o: It interferes with the intestinal cellular uptake of dietary calcium and vitamin D
It acts primarily as a bone-softening agent that leads to osteomalacia-like changes
It directly stimulates osteoclast activity via the suppression of endogenous calcitonin
It has been linked to an increased risk for breast cancer and venous thromboembolism
qs.e: Estrogen-progestin therapy is no longer considered first-line because it has been linked to an increased risk for breast cancer, stroke, venous thromboembolism, and coronary disease. Estrogen is now recommended primarily if patients seek relief of postmenopausal symptoms.

qs.q: Which disease of bone is managed using hormone replacement therapy to counteract decreased bone mass?
qs.e: Osteoporosis features significant decreases in bone mass and is commonly treated with bisphosphonates and hormone replacement therapy. Paget's disease involves disorganized bone remodeling rather than standard postmenopausal bone loss.
